# Abstract

Between 1000AD and 1500AD the Near East, the Iranian plateau, Afghanistan, Caucasia and the Arabian Peninsula moved from late Abbasid agrarian maturity through Turkic migration, Crusader warfare, Mongol conquest and pandemic plague to a fractured but resilient late mediaeval recovery. Across the eight sub-regions encompassing 6,78M km², aggregate population stood at 37,7M in 1000AD and edged to a pre-Mongol crest of 37,82M in 1150AD as Seljuk Iran, Bagratid Georgia and Ghurid Khorasan expanded even while Byzantine-Seljuk conflict trimmed Anatolia and canal decay eroded lower Iraq. The thirteenth-century Mongol campaigns in Khorasan and Mesopotamia, followed by Hulagu's sack of Baghdad in 1258AD, Ilkhanid pastoral conversion and the Black Death of 1347-1349AD, cut the macro-regional total to 32,48M in 1250AD and to a trough of 25M in 1350AD, roughly one third below the twelfth-century peak. Over the final century and a half, despite Timur's destructive campaigns across Iran, Iraq and eastern Anatolia between 1380AD and 1402AD, recovery in Timurid Herat, Qara Qoyunlu and Aq Qoyunlu Tabriz, rising Ottoman western Anatolia and Rasulid Yemen lifted the regional total back to 28,74M by 1500AD. Combining 2.381 mediaeval archaeological and chronometric sites across 1.311 active Voronoi catchments with non-stationary Matérn kriging, 66.671 individually assessed mediaeval settlements and backward-calibrated subadministrative benchmarks from 29 historical Ottoman, Russian and Mandate divisions alongside 2.629 modern districts, HANDBOOK reconstructs the demographic redistribution between irrigated river plains, highland refuges and semi-arid steppe frontiers across five turbulent centuries.



# Background

The half-millennium from 1000AD to 1500AD marks the decisive structural divide in the demographic history of southwestern Asia. At the opening of the eleventh century, the Islamic world from the Zagros mountains to the Syrian steppe still rested on the urban and hydraulic foundations laid under late Antiquity and the early Caliphate. Buyid Iran, Samanid and Ghaznavid Khorasan, Fatimid Syria and Byzantine Anatolia each sustained dense networks of market towns, caravan stages and canal-fed villages, even though the great alluvial plain of southern Iraq had already begun to contract from its early Abbasid zenith [@Mahmuluddin2024Myth; @Bosworth2007Historic]. Over the ensuing five centuries, however, successive waves of nomadic pastoralist incursion, frontier warfare and epidemic mortality reshaped where people could live and how much surplus rural agriculture could support. Unlike earlier imperial consolidations that absorbed peripheral peoples into existing agrarian tax bases, the Seljuk, Khwarazmian, Mongol Ilkhanid and Timurid regimes repeatedly shifted the balance of land use between settled ploughland and seasonal grazing across the Anatolian plateau, the Armenian highlands, Azerbaijan and northeastern Iran [@Peacock2021Urban; @Katie2021Cities; @Wing2016Jalayirids].

## Ecological Zones and Agrarian Foundations

Geography dictates the demographic ceiling across this 6,78M km² expanse. Rainfall agriculture above the 300 mm isohyet forms an irregular arc stretching from western and northern Anatolia through the Pontic and Taurus ranges, across northern Syria and Upper Mesopotamia, up into the Transcaucasian valleys of Georgia, Armenia and Shirvan, and along the Caspian littoral of Gilan and Mazandaran. Everywhere else, dense human settlement depended on engineered water: river-diversion canals along the Tigris, Euphrates, Orontes and Helmand; subterranean *qanat* chains tapping alluvial fans around the rim of the Iranian plateau; mountain terraces in Yemen, Oman and Mount Lebanon; and oasis springs scattered across Hijaz, Najd and eastern Arabia [@AM2026Tale; @P2020Climate; @M2022Using]. Where political stability kept *qanat* galleries clear of silt and canal headworks repaired, oasis hinterlands around Nishapur, Rayy, Isfahan, Shiraz, Herat and Damascus supported urban populations running into the tens of thousands. Where protracted warfare interrupted maintenance or pushed cultivators off the plains, desert scrub and brackish marshland reclaimed once-fertile districts within a single generation.

Anatolia and Transcaucasia presented a starkly different ecological profile. The central Anatolian steppe around Konya, Aksaray and Kayseri experienced cold winters and modest rainfall, favouring extensive cereal cultivation mixed with transhumant sheep and goat herding [@M2026Late; @Peacock2021Urban]. After the Seljuk victory at Manzikert in 1071AD opened the interior plateau to Oghuz Turcoman tribes, rural settlement thinned in exposed river valleys while fortified towns and caravanserai corridors consolidated along the Konya-Sivas-Erzurum trunk road [@Peacock2021Urban; @S2020History]. Further east, the Kingdom of Georgia and adjacent Armenian and Shirvani principalities occupied tightly partitioned valleys along the Kura and Rioni basins. Under David IV (r. 1089-1125AD) and Queen Tamar (r. 1184-1213AD), Bagratid consolidation secured the lowland pastures and trade arteries connecting Tiflis (Tbilisi), Ani and Ganja, allowing Caucasia's population to climb above 3M before thirteenth-century Khwarazmian and Mongol raids disrupted the southern marches [@Guven2024Seljuk; @Yusif2025Reflection; @Macharashvili2025Types].

## Political Shocks from Manzikert to Timur

Four major political and epidemiological shocks governed the trajectory between 1000AD and 1500AD. First, the eleventh-century Seljuk expansion transformed the ethnic and fiscal geography of Iran, Iraq, Syria and Anatolia, culminating in the establishment of the Rum Sultanate at Konya and a patchwork of Artuqid, Danishmendid and Zengid atabegates across the Jazira and northern Levant [@Peacock2021Urban; @Guven2024Seljuk]. In the Levant itself, two centuries of Crusader-Ayyubid and Mamluk contestation devastated coastal ports such as Ascalon, Acre and Sidon while inland Damascus and Aleppo retained commercial vitality through caravan and grain trade [@RNR2021Weapon; @M2020Genetic; @A2002Book].

Second, the Mongol invasions struck in two devastating pulses: Genghis Khan's 1219-1223AD assault on Transoxiana, Khorasan and eastern Afghanistan, which shattered Marv, Nishapur, Balkh and Herat [@Katie2021Cities; @Bosworth2007Historic], and Hulagu Khan's 1256-1260AD campaign, which terminated the Abbasid Caliphate in Baghdad in 1258AD and raided northern Syria [@Wing2016Jalayirids]. Archaeological stratigraphy from Khorasan and Central Asia confirms sharp urban contraction and abandonment of suburban quarters, even though recovery began selectively in administrative hubs once Ilkhanid rule stabilised under Ghazan Khan (r. 1295-1304AD) [@Katie2021Cities; @Darvish2025Comparativ].

Third, the second plague pandemic struck the Near East in 1347-1349AD via maritime links from the Black Sea to Constantinople, Cyprus, Alexandria and the Levantine coast, as well as overland corridors tied to Mongol-era focalisation across western Eurasia [@MH2025Plague]. Repeated recurrences through the late fourteenth and fifteenth centuries prevented rapid demographic rebound in Egypt, Syria, Iraq and Cyprus, leaving rural labour scarce and urban tax rolls depressed [@Idiman2022Tributary; @W1997Book].

Fourth, Timur's campaigns between 1380AD and 1402AD inflicted renewed siege destruction on Isfahan, Shiraz, Baghdad, Aleppo, Damascus and Georgia, and broke Ottoman expansion temporarily at Ankara in 1402AD [@Wing2016Jalayirids; @Yusif2025Reflection]. Yet the fifteenth century was not uniformly bleak. Under Shah Rukh in Herat, the Qara Qoyunlu and Aq Qoyunlu rulers in Tabriz, and the rebuilding Ottoman state in western and central Anatolia, regional trade, irrigation repair and architectural patronage initiated a sustained upward turn that carried total population from 25M in 1350AD to 28,74M in 1500AD [@Darvish2025Comparativ; @Idiman2022Tributary].

## Hydraulic Infrastructure, Pastoralisation and Urban Institutions

Across arid and semi-arid basins, political instability translated into demographic loss primarily through the disruption of waterworks and fiscal tenure rather than battlefield casualties alone. Under the Great Seljuks and their successor dynasties, the spread of *iqta* revenue assignments tied military commanders directly to rural districts, encouraging short-term extraction whenever central oversight weakened. In southern Iraq, repeated breaches along the Nahrawan and Tigris levees combined with brackish waterlogging to reduce the cultivated area of the Sawad long before 1258AD [@Bosworth2007Historic; @Wing2016Jalayirids]. Across the Iranian plateau, by contrast, underground *qanat* galleries required continuous annual clearing by specialised village crews; once Mongol sieges dispersed rural labour in Nishapur, Tus and Marv, dry alluvial fans reverted to seasonal steppe within decades [@Katie2021Cities].

At the same time, pious endowments (*waqf*) buffered major urban nuclei against prolonged fiscal collapse. In Rum Seljuk Anatolia, Syria and Timurid Khorasan, sultans and urban notables endowed madrasas, hospitals (*darüşşifa*), public baths and fortified stone caravanserais linked to commercial bazaars and rural estates [@Peacock2021Urban; @S2020History; @Mahmuluddin2024Myth]. These institutions concentrated artisans, scholars and merchants inside walled cores at Konya, Kayseri, Sivas, Aleppo, Damascus, Tabriz and Herat, explaining why key regional capitals recovered far faster after conquest or epidemic mortality than surrounding open villages [@Darvish2025Comparativ].

# Methodology

Reconstructing regional population totals across five mediaeval centuries requires bridging an evidentiary chasm: neither the Rum Seljuk sultanate nor Ilkhanid Iran nor Rasulid Yemen left surviving empire-wide household censuses comparable to early modern Ottoman *tahrir* registers or nineteenth-century Imperial counts. HANDBOOK therefore adopts Regime 2 reconstruction, anchoring the 1000-1500AD trajectory between the classical-early Islamic baseline below and the sixteenth-to-twentieth-century administrative censuses above, while allocating people across space through archaeological site surfaces, settlement rank-size patterns and ecological covariates.

## Sub-Regional Partition and Boundary Harmonisation

The macro-region is partitioned into eight contiguous or insular sub-regions covering 6.784.376 km² in total spherical area, bounded along mountain watersheds, desert margins and maritime coastlines rather than modern national borders alone. The largest territorial unit is the Arabian Peninsula (Rasulid Yemen, Nabhanid Oman and Hijaz-Najd, 2.793.199 km²), followed by the Iranian plateau (Seljuk, Khwarazmian, Ilkhanid and Timurid Iran, 1.623.347 km²), Rum Seljuk and Beylik Anatolia (779.615 km²), Ghaznavid, Ghurid and Timurid Afghanistan (642.476 km²), Seljuk, Ilkhanid and Jalayirid Iraq (437.722 km²), the Crusader, Ayyubid and Mamluk Levant (313.332 km²), the Kingdom of Georgia, Armenia and Shirvan (185.338 km²) and Byzantine and Lusignan Cyprus (9.346 km²). All polygons are maintained as smooth vector boundaries and projected in upright Lambert Azimuthal Equal-Area coordinates centred on the Near Eastern core so that areal calculations and cartographic panels suffer zero high-latitude or equirectangular stretching.

## Archaeological Catchment Disaggregation and Matérn Kriging

To distribute regional populations across rural and urban landscapes without projecting modern metropolis footprints backwards into the Middle Ages, HANDBOOK draws on a pan-regional archaeological register comprising 83.857,2 weighted domestic sites across 3.416 Voronoi catchments (median catchment radius 32,51 km; 90th percentile 40,25 km). Within the mediaeval horizon, 2.381 dated archaeological and historical site records occupy 1.311 active domestic catchments across 68.198 valid inhabited grid cells. Each site record originates from verified regional surveys, excavated site atlases, early Islamic geographic itineraries and radiocarbon compendia rather than unvetted crowd-sourced gazetteers [@Abballe2022Medieval; @M2026Late; @AM2026Tale].

Spatial interpolation employs parameter-free Freeman-Tukey variance stabilisation paired with two-scale non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) residual kriging over metric-isotropic radial geodesic distances between Voronoi catchment centroids. Environmental conditioning incorporates five weighted-least-squares covariates: baseline habitability ($\beta_0 = 0,01$), natural net primary productivity ($\beta_1 = 0,01$), ecological suitability ($\beta_2 = 0,01$), fluvial proximity ($\beta_3 = 0,046$) and coastal proximity ($\beta_4 = 0,042$). The elevated fluvial and coastal weights accurately reflect mediaeval settlement clustering along the Tigris, Euphrates, Kura, Orontes and Levantine littoral. An explicit urban mask with a two-cell buffer isolates dense historic urban cores from adjacent rural catchments, preventing modern agglomerations such as Tehran, Riyadh or contemporary Istanbul from distorting mediaeval countryside gradients.

## Subadministrative GIS Disaggregation and Pycnophylactic Scaling

Longitudinal continuity across the 1500AD boundary links the mediaeval horizon directly to nineteenth- and twentieth-century administrative enumerations through strictly mass-conserving pycnophylactic scaling. Historical administrative polygons for 29 sub-national divisions - spanning late Ottoman vilayets across Anatolia, Syria, Lebanon, Palestine, Transjordan and Iraq, Russian Imperial guberniyas of Tiflis, Kutais, Erivan, Baku and Elizavetpol in Transcaucasia, and the six British colonial districts of Cyprus - are paired with 2.629 modern ADM1 and ADM2 polygons obtained from the geoBoundaries global political boundary archive [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries]. Disaggregation across 83 benchmark years yields 65.864 unit-year mass checks in which every polygon preserves its recorded census population over the underlying dasymetric habitability raster.

## Settlement Catalogue and Rank-Size Calibration

Urban centres anchor the upper tail of the population distribution and provide point-level historical controls against chronicle figures and excavated wall circuits. The mediaeval settlement gazetteer synthesises 66.671 individually assessed settlements (selected after screening 66.921 candidate places in the source ledger and excluding 250 co-located localities, variant-spelling duplicates, non-settlement fragments or unquantified minor scatters) from excavated wall-circuit surveys, early Islamic geographical compendia and historical settlement registers (including Al-Thurayya, DARMC, Euratlas and regional Anatolian and Near Eastern survey corpora), Crusader and Mamluk administrative records and late fifteenth-century Ottoman *tahrir* registers [@Bosworth2007Historic; @Katie2021Cities; @Yusif2025Reflection]. Each settlement carries a case-by-case population series spanning its documented occupation between 1000AD and 1500AD, incorporating event-year benchmarks for major sacks and epidemics, and is ranked by peak population to test conformity with Zipf's rank-size law where sample sizes exceed the minimum threshold of 25 places.

# Testing and Validation

Model integrity across HANDBOOK's mediaeval horizon is evaluated along three independent axes: variogram calibration of the Matérn kriging surface, exact mass conservation across historical and modern administrative polygons, and settlement rank-size behaviour across the 66.671 individually assessed urban and rural nodes.

## Matérn Semivariogram Diagnostics

Empirical semivariance across dimensionless Voronoi geodesic lags ($u_{ij}$) for the mediaeval horizon confirms strong spatial coherence at local and regional scales. Normalised semivariance climbs smoothly from $\gamma(u) = 0,000005$ at $u = 0,42$ to $0,000061$ at $u = 1,61$ and approaches its regional sill of $0,000127$ by $u = 7,8$. The fitted two-component Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) model achieves a weighted-least-squares coefficient of determination of $R^2 = 0,999$, with raw short-range parameter $\tau_1 = 1,505$ regularised to $\tau_1 = 1,35$ (corresponding to an effective short spatial correlation range of 48,93 km) and secondary scale $\tau_2 = 2,903$ under component weights $c_1 = 0,8$ and $c_2 = 0,2$. Regularising the nugget-to-sill ratio to $\eta = 0,04$ eliminates isolated single-catchment spikes while preserving sharp gradients along irrigated river valleys and mountain foothills.

## Pycnophylactic Mass Conservation and Subadministrative Coverage

Across the complete HANDBOOK domain, disaggregation of the 29 historical subadministrative units and 2.629 modern geoBoundaries units [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries] across 83 benchmark years passes all 65.864 unit-year conservation checks within 0,01% tolerance, recording a global maximum relative error of $5,85 \times 10^{-8}$. Within Chapter 8's territories, late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century subadministrative series provide an empirical anchor for regional shares: Anatolia's seven Ottoman vilayet groupings enumerated 11,29M inhabitants in 1881AD and 14,17M in 1914AD before war and displacement reduced eastern vilayets sharply by 1927AD; the three Iraqi vilayets of Baghdad, Basra and Mosul rose from 1,8M in 1881AD to 2,93M in 1920AD and 4,82M by 1947AD; and Transcaucasia's five Russian guberniyas grew from 3,76M in 1886AD to 5,94M in 1914AD. Modern geoBoundaries coverage spans 968 ADM2 districts in Turkey, 379 in Iran, 355 in Afghanistan, 136 in Saudi Arabia, 88 in Iraq, 78 in Azerbaijan, 61 in Georgia, 53 in Oman, 21 each in Lebanon and Yemen, 16 in Palestine, 14 in Israel, 13 ADM1 governorates in Syria, 12 in Jordan, 11 in Armenia and 5 in Cyprus.

## Settlement Rank-Size Integrity

Evaluating all 66.671 individually assessed mediaeval settlements yields a Zipf rank-size slope of $\alpha = 1,02$ ($R^2 = 0,88$). This close conformity to canonical Zipfian scaling across tens of thousands of urban and regional nodes reflects two structural realities of mediaeval southwestern Asia: first, successive imperial capitals achieved true metropolitan scale - led by late Abbasid Baghdad (284k in 1200AD), Ilkhanid and Turkmen Tabriz (235k in 1340AD), Timurid Herat (152k in 1500AD), pre-Mongol Nishapur (132k in 1050AD), Ghaznavid Ghazni (128k in 1050AD), Seljuk Isfahan (112k in 1100AD), Mamluk Damascus (108,5k in 1340AD) and Seljuk Rayy (108k in 1050AD); second, competing regional dynasties sustained a broad second tier between 50k and 95k - including Balkh (94k), Mosul (94k), Shiraz (93,5k), Aleppo (91k), Konya (86k), Ani (84,5k), Sultaniyya (84k) and Tbilisi (78,5k) - anchored above hundreds of secondary market towns and caravan stages rather than collapsing into a single primate city [@Katie2021Cities; @Wing2016Jalayirids; @Peacock2021Urban].

# Results

Between 1000AD and 1500AD, aggregate population across the eight sub-regions traced a distinct plateau, deep contraction and partial recovery: 37,7M in 1000AD, 37,82M in 1150AD, 32,48M in 1250AD, 25M in 1350AD and 28,74M in 1500AD. Beneath this headline curve, however, individual sub-regions diverged sharply in timing and magnitude depending on exposure to nomadic conquest, irrigation fragility and maritime plague corridors.

## Rum Seljuk and Beylik Anatolia (1000-1500AD)

Anatolia opened the eleventh century with roughly 8,95M inhabitants (11,5 persons per km²), making it the second most populous unit in the macro-region after Iran. Byzantine provincial stability under Basil II sustained dense village settlement across the Aegean river valleys, Bithynia, Cappadocia and the Pontic coast [@M2026Late]. Following the Seljuk breakthrough after 1071AD, prolonged frontier raiding across the central plateau and western river valleys reduced the Anatolian population to 8,15M by 1150AD, a drop of nearly 9%. Once the Rum Sultanate consolidated around Konya, Kayseri and Sivas under Kilij Arslan II and his thirteenth-century successors, however, agricultural recovery, Black Sea and Mediterranean port treaties, and an ambitious network of stone caravanserais and urban pious endowments lifted Anatolia back to 8,45M by 1250AD [@Peacock2021Urban; @S2020History]. The Mongol defeat of the Seljuks at Köse Dağ in 1243AD initially imposed tributary demands rather than wholesale massacre, but subsequent Ilkhanid fiscal collapse, Turkmen principalities (*beyliks*) skirmishing across western frontiers and the Black Death of 1347-1349AD lowered the peninsula to 6,85M in 1350AD [@Peacock2021Urban; @MH2025Plague]. Despite Timur's invasion of 1402AD, Ottoman consolidation across Bithynia, Mysia and the central plateau restored security over rural arable land, bringing Anatolia back to 7,95M by 1500AD - once again the largest single sub-region in the Near East [@Idiman2022Tributary].

## Crusader, Ayyubid and Mamluk Levant and Cyprus

The Levant (Syria, Lebanon, Palestine and Jordan) held 4,15M inhabitants in 1000AD (13,2 persons per km², the highest regional density on the mainland) and 4,05M in 1150AD. Crusader conquest along the littoral from Antioch to Jerusalem redistributed rural surpluses through Frankish lordships while triggering periodic massacres and sieges in coastal ports such as Sidon, Tyre and Acre [@RNR2021Weapon; @M2020Genetic]. Under Saladin and the Ayyubids, and subsequently under Mamluk integration with Egypt after 1260AD, interior cities such as Damascus and Aleppo remained commercial hubs even as Mamluk coastal scorched-earth policy dismantled Frankish port fortifications to deter renewed seaborne crusades [@A2002Book; @W1997Book]. Consequently, Levantine numbers drifted down to 3,75M in 1250AD before plunging to 2,65M in 1350AD under the twin blows of plague mortality and Euphrates frontier insecurity [@MH2025Plague]. A modest fifteenth-century stabilisation raised the Levant to 2,95M by 1500AD. Offshore, Byzantine and Lusignan Cyprus followed a parallel maritime rhythm: rising from 200k in 1000AD to 215k in 1150AD and 225k in 1250AD (24,1 persons per km²) as sugar estates and Levantine refugees boosted Famagusta and Nicosia, then collapsing by a third to 150k in 1350AD under plague before recovering to 185k by 1500AD [@Kaya2016History].

## Kingdom of Georgia, Armenia and Shirvan

Transcaucasia experienced one of the sharpest twelfth-century expansions anywhere in southwestern Asia. From 2,65M in 1000AD, the combined population of Georgia, Armenia and Shirvan climbed to 3,15M in 1150AD (+18,9%, reaching 17 persons per km²). Bagratid kings cleared banditry from lowland valleys, resettled highland clans along the Kura corridor, fortified Tbilisi and patronised thriving artisan and merchant quarters in Ani and Ganja [@Yusif2025Reflection; @Guven2024Seljuk; @Macharashvili2025Types]. Even a catastrophic earthquake at Ganja in 1139AD did not arrest the region's broader urban growth [@Yusif2025Reflection]. That golden age broke abruptly in the 1220s and 1230s under Jalal al-Din Khwarazmshah's devastating invasions and the Mongol occupation of Armenia and eastern Georgia, pulling Caucasia down to 2,85M by 1250AD. Further plague outbreaks and Timur's eight Caucasian campaigns between 1386AD and 1403AD reduced the region to 2,15M in 1350AD before fifteenth-century recovery under Georgian principalities and Shirvanshah rule lifted the total to 2,45M by 1500AD [@Yusif2025Reflection; @Guven2024Seljuk].

## Iran, Iraq and Afghanistan: From Seljuk Zenith to Mongol and Timurid Reconstruction

Iran, Iraq and Afghanistan absorbed the brunt of Central Asian steppe conquests. At the opening of the eleventh century, Iran held 9,35M people and expanded under Great Seljuk administration to a mediaeval peak of 9,85M by 1150AD, anchored by large oasis and plateau metropolises at Nishapur, Rayy, Isfahan, Shiraz and Hamadan [@Mahmuluddin2024Myth; @Bosworth2007Historic]. Ghaznavid and Ghurid Afghanistan similarly rose from 3,15M in 1000AD to 3,45M in 1150AD as Herat, Ghazni and Balkh prospered along the trans-Khorasan caravan routes [@Hannan2025Sufic; @Katie2021Cities]. Iraq, by contrast, continued a slow structural contraction from 5,6M in 1000AD to 5,1M in 1150AD as salinisation and political factionalism around Baghdad eroded the Sawad's ancient canal grid.

Between 1219AD and 1258AD, the Mongol onslaught broke this agrarian order. Khorasan and Transoxiana suffered systematic siege slaughter and *qanat* destruction under Genghis Khan's armies, cutting Iran from 9,85M to 6,95M and Afghanistan from 3,45M to 2,35M by 1250AD [@Katie2021Cities]. In Iraq, Hulagu's sack of Baghdad in 1258AD compounded decades of neglect along the Diyala and lower Euphrates canals, reducing Iraq to 3,85M in 1250AD and just 2,35M in 1350AD - less than half its 1000AD population [@Wing2016Jalayirids]. Iran fell further to 5,45M and Afghanistan to 2,05M in 1350AD under Ilkhanid collapse and plague [@MH2025Plague]. Yet reconstruction did follow. Under the Jalayirids in Baghdad and Tabriz, the Aq Qoyunlu in Azerbaijan and Shah Rukh's Timurid renaissance in Herat, urban ateliers, Madrasas and irrigation channels revived selectively, raising Iran to 6,35M, Afghanistan to 2,65M and Iraq marginally to 2,45M by 1500AD [@Wing2016Jalayirids; @Darvish2025Comparativ].

## The Arabian Peninsula

Across Arabia (2.793.199 km²), low overall density (roughly 1,3 persons per km²) masked concentrated agricultural populations in the terraced highlands of Yemen, the falaj-irrigated valleys of Oman and the oases of Hijaz and Najd. Under Sulayhid and Rasulid stability in Yemen and steady Indian Ocean spice-trade revenues through Aden, Arabia grew steadily from 3,65M in 1000AD to 3,85M in 1150AD and 4,05M in 1250AD before mid-fourteenth-century plague and arid-zone volatility trimmed it to 3,35M in 1350AD. Fifteenth-century Tahirid and Nabhanid continuity restored the peninsula to 3,75M by 1500AD, slightly above its 1000AD starting level.

## Cross-Regional Divergence: Highland Refuges versus Alluvial Plains

Comparing all eight sub-regions across the five-century span reveals a sharp structural contrast between mountain-and-maritime peripheries and open alluvial lowlands. By 1500AD, Arabia stood 2,7% above its 1000AD population, Cyprus had recovered to within 7,5% of its eleventh-century baseline, Caucasia stood 7,5% below 1000AD and Anatolia 11,2% below 1000AD. Highland terraces, rain-fed coastal valleys and fortified mountain passes buffered peasant communities against wholesale nomadisation and allowed rapid recolonisation once major campaigns passed [@Guven2024Seljuk; @Peacock2021Urban].

By contrast, open hydraulic plains suffered severe long-term hysteresis. Over the same half-millennium, Iran fell by 32,1% (from 9,35M to 6,35M), the Levant by 28,9% (from 4,15M to 2,95M) and Iraq by 56,3% (from 5,6M to 2,45M). Repeated Mongol and Timurid campaigns destroyed urban craft quarters along flat caravan routes, while mid-fourteenth-century plague decimated dense riverine populations and left canal networks starved of maintenance labour [@Katie2021Cities; @Wing2016Jalayirids; @MH2025Plague]. The demographic centre of gravity of southwestern Asia accordingly shifted north-westwards from lower Mesopotamia and eastern Khorasan towards Anatolia, Azerbaijan and the northern Syrian-Lebanese arc.

# Limitations

Three evidentiary constraints bound the precision of these estimates. First, quantitative survival is highly uneven across regions and centuries. While eleventh- and twelfth-century Arabic geographers provide detailed itinerary hierarchies for Iran, Iraq and Syria, quantitative fiscal series for rural Anatolia, highland Georgia, Ghurid Afghanistan and interior Najd before 1500AD remain fragmentary [@Bosworth2007Historic; @Peacock2021Urban]. Urban chronicler tallies - particularly siege casualty figures under the Mongols and Timur - routinely exaggerate populations by factors of three to ten and cannot be taken literally without archaeological wall-circuit and residential-density cross-checks [@Katie2021Cities].

Second, plague mortality between 1347AD and 1500AD varied sharply between coastal entrepôts, caravan corridors and isolated highland valleys [@MH2025Plague]. Because fifty-year benchmark intervals smooth over sharp decennial epidemics and localized famines, the 1350AD figures capture net mid-century troughs rather than instantaneous annual death spikes. Third, archaeological survey intensity remains higher in Israel, Jordan, western Turkey and parts of northern Iraq than in eastern Iran, southern Arabia or conflict-affected provinces of Afghanistan and Syria; although HANDBOOK's Voronoi centroid kriging dampens raw survey-cluster bias, rural density surfaces in lightly surveyed arid basins carry wider uncertainty envelopes (10% to 20%) than along well-excavated Levantine and Mesopotamian river valleys [@Abballe2022Medieval; @P2020Climate].

# Conclusion

Between 1000AD and 1500AD, the population of the Near East, Iran, Afghanistan, Caucasia and Arabia declined by nearly a quarter overall, from 37,7M to 28,74M, after touching a deep mid-fourteenth-century trough of 25M. That aggregate fall was neither uniform nor irreversible. Until 1150AD, expansion across Seljuk Iran, Bagratid Georgia and Ghurid Khorasan offset early losses in Anatolia and southern Iraq, holding the macro-region near 37,82M. Thereafter, Mongol siege warfare, hydraulic neglect in Iraq, Ilkhanid pastoralisation and the arrival of the Black Death broke the demographic parity that southwestern Asia had maintained with western Europe and East Asia since Antiquity. Iraq never recovered its mediaeval losses before the nineteenth century, whereas Anatolia, western Iran, Herat and Yemen mounted a durable fifteenth-century rebound that laid the demographic base for the early modern Ottoman and Safavid empires [@Idiman2022Tributary; @Darvish2025Comparativ].
